blocks.content: Coastal zones represent dynamic interface environments where terrestrial and marine processes interact, serving as vital ecological buffers and drivers of the national maritime economy.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Coastal zones represent dynamic interface areas where terrestrial and marine processes interact, supporting high biodiversity ecosystems like mangroves and coral reefs.
They act as natural protection buffers against extreme marine hazards, including storm surges, cyclones, tsunamis, and coastal erosion.
Coastal regions are central to the national 'Blue Economy', hosting vital ports, shipping lanes, fisheries, tourism, and offshore oil and mineral reserves.
India manages coastal development through the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notifications, which classify shorelines to balance ecological protection with economic activities.

rows: No new construction permitted except pipeline laying, radar installation, and essential public facilities.
Construction permitted on the landward side of existing authorized roads or approved structures.
Divided into CRZ-III A (High density population; NDZ of 50m) and CRZ-III B (Low density population; NDZ of 200m).

No restriction on traditional fishing; strictly regulates dumping of untreated sewage, solid waste, and effluents.

items: India's total coastline extends over 7,516.6 km, spanning 9 coastal states (Gujarat having the longest coastline) and 4 island/coastal Union Territories.
Under CRZ Notification 2018, CRZ-I A covers Ecologically Sensitive Areas (ESAs) like mangroves, corals, and sand dunes where construction is strictly regulated.
The Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) extends from the baseline up to 200 nautical miles, conferring sovereign rights over natural resource exploration.
